Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Marcus is a twenty-nine-year-old salesperson living in a mid-sized Midwestern city, a job that once felt natural to him—talking to people, building rapport, closing deals. He grew up in a small town near a river, spending his childhood summers fishing and hiking in the woods that bordered the floodplain. That changed two years ago, when a sudden, catastrophic flood swept through the region after days of relentless rain. Marcus was at home when the water began rising faster than anyone had anticipated. He remembers the sound first—a low, grinding roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once—and then the brown, debris-filled water crashing through his ground-floor apartment. He scrambled onto the roof, clinging to a vent pipe for hours as the current tore past, carrying cars, trees, and parts of houses. What he cannot remember, no matter how hard he tries, is the face of the neighbor who screamed for help from a nearby rooftop. He knows she was there, he knows he heard her, but the image is gone, replaced only by the sickening feeling of his own terror and the certainty that he did nothing. When the water receded and rescue came, Marcus was alive, but something inside him had been washed away.

In the weeks and months that followed, Marcus found himself unable to return to his apartment. He moved to a new building on the other side of town, on high ground, far from the river. He told himself it was practical, a fresh start. But soon he noticed he could no longer stand the sound of rain. A sudden downpour would send his heart racing, his palms slick with sweat, and he would find himself checking the weather app obsessively, scanning for flood warnings even on clear days. He began to avoid the natural environment altogether—parks, wooded trails, even the manicured green spaces near his office. Walking past a pond or a creek made his chest tighten, as if the earth itself might open up again. At night, he would wake abruptly, sitting up in bed, listening for the sound of rushing water, his body poised to run. He would then walk through his apartment, checking the doors, the windows, the drains, assuring himself that the floor was dry, before he could lie down again.

At work, Marcus’s easy confidence eroded. He found himself on edge during meetings, scanning the room for exits, his attention splintering whenever a colleague’s voice grew sharp or urgent. He began to interpret small gestures—a client’s hesitation, a manager’s offhand comment—as signs that he was about to be abandoned or blamed. He came to believe that he could not rely on other people, that they would only let him down or, worse, reveal his own failure. He stopped joining his coworkers for after-work drinks, avoided team-building events, and let his sales pipeline dwindle. His manager noticed, but Marcus could not explain why he felt so brittle, so close to breaking.

What frightened Marcus most, though, was the way the terror returned without warning. He would be sitting at his desk, staring at a spreadsheet, and suddenly his chest would seize, his breath would go shallow, and he would feel the same raw, animal panic he had felt on that rooftop—but there was no image, no memory, just the emotion flooding through him like a wave. Other times, when he deliberately tried to recall the flood, the memory hit him with the full force of the original event, leaving him shaking and disoriented. He had come to feel like a stranger to himself. The person he used to be—confident, sociable, sure of his place in the world—felt like a ghost. Nothing in his life seemed meaningful anymore. His job was just a series of motions, his friendships hollow, his evenings empty. He had stopped dating entirely, certain that no one could understand what he carried.

Marcus finally sought help after a minor incident: a clogged sink at his apartment that overflowed onto the bathroom floor. He stood in the doorway, staring at the inch of water, unable to move, his heart hammering, until his neighbor heard his shouts and turned off the valve. That night, he googled trauma therapy and made an appointment. He is afraid of what he might find if he looks too closely at those hours on the roof, but he is more afraid of spending the rest of his life checking for water in the dark.
